q: How do you use short-lived OIDC tokens in CI to eliminate stored cloud secrets?
p: The CI platform issues a signed identity token per job; the cloud trusts that issuer and exchanges the token for temporary credentials. Trust conditions on repo, branch and environment limit who can assume the role.
cmds: gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe ci --workload-identity-pool=pool --location=global
tip: The subject claim in the trust policy is the security boundary. A wildcard there lets any repository assume the role.
a: Static cloud keys stored as CI secrets are a standing target: they leak through logs, forks and compromised runners, and they rarely get rotated. With OIDC federation, each pipeline job receives a short-lived signed token that states which repository, branch and workflow it belongs to. In the cloud I register the CI platform as a trusted identity provider and create a role whose trust policy accepts tokens only when claims match, for example the exact repository and the main branch or a protected deployment environment. The job exchanges the token for temporary credentials valid for minutes, so there is nothing long-lived to steal. I separate roles by purpose, with a read-only role for pull request builds and a deploy role for protected branches, and I scope permissions tightly. The common mistake is a loose subject condition, which lets other repositories in the organisation assume the role, so I test the policy with negative cases.
f: Why separate roles for pull requests?

q: What is the Secrets Store CSI Driver and how does it differ from External Secrets Operator?
p: The CSI driver mounts secrets from a provider directly into pods as files at start time, optionally syncing to a Kubernetes Secret. ESO continuously syncs external secrets into native Secret objects. Pick by whether you want files or Secret objects.
cmds: volumes: - name: sec csi: driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io readOnly: true
tip: CSI mounting can avoid storing the value in etcd at all, which is its main security advantage.
a: Both bring secrets from a manager such as Vault or a cloud service into Kubernetes, but they work differently. The Secrets Store CSI driver uses a volume: when a pod starts, the driver authenticates with the pod's identity, fetches the listed secrets and mounts them as files in a memory-backed volume. Rotation can be handled by periodic refresh of the mount. By default the value never becomes a Kubernetes Secret, so it is not stored in etcd, although it can optionally be synced to one for environment variable use. External Secrets Operator instead runs a controller that reads from the external store and creates or updates ordinary Secret objects, which any workload can consume in the usual ways, and it handles refresh intervals and templating well. I choose CSI when minimising exposure in etcd matters or apps read files, and ESO when applications and tools expect native Secrets, such as Ingress TLS.
f: When do secrets land in etcd?
How does rotation reach a running pod?

q: How do you handle secrets in Docker builds without baking them into image layers?
p: Use BuildKit secret mounts or SSH mounts, which expose the secret only during one RUN step and leave nothing in layers or history. Never use ARG or ENV for credentials, and use multi-stage builds.
tip: Deleting a file in a later layer does not remove it from the earlier layer. Anyone with the image can extract it.
a: Image layers are permanent, and anyone who can pull the image can read every layer, so a secret copied in during build is exposed even if a later step deletes it. Build arguments and environment variables are also recorded in the image history. The correct tool is BuildKit's secret mount: the secret is supplied at build time from a file or environment on the builder, appears at a path under run secrets only during the single instruction that mounts it, and is never written to a layer. For private Git dependencies, an SSH mount forwards the agent socket in the same transient way. I also use multi-stage builds, so credentials only exist in a builder stage that is discarded, and scan the final image and its history for secrets. The runtime secrets are not baked in at all; they are injected by the platform when the container starts.
f: Why doesn't deleting a file help?
What is a multi-stage build's role here?

q: How do you design a break-glass process for secrets and privileged access?
p: A documented emergency path with strong authentication, time-boxed elevated access, mandatory justification, alerting, session recording, and automatic credential rotation afterwards. Test it regularly so it works under pressure.
tip: Every break-glass use should page the security team and generate a review ticket. Silent use defeats the purpose.
a: Normal access controls sometimes block legitimate emergency work, for example when the identity provider is down or a production incident needs temporary elevated rights. Break-glass is the controlled exception. The credentials are stored offline or in a vault with split custody, and using them requires multi-person approval or at least a strong second factor. Access is time-limited, so it expires automatically, and requires a stated reason linked to an incident. Using the account triggers an immediate alert to the security team, sessions are recorded or logged in detail, and after the emergency the credentials are rotated and the usage is reviewed within a day or two. I test the procedure regularly, because an untested emergency path often fails when needed, and verify that the monitoring really fires. The accounts are excluded from daily use and from routine automation to keep the signal clean.
f: Why must use trigger an alert?
How often would you test break-glass?

q: What is secret zero and how do you solve the bootstrap problem?
p: Any system that fetches secrets needs an initial credential. Solve it with platform identity: cloud instance or workload identity, Kubernetes service account tokens, or attestation, so no static bootstrap secret is distributed.
cmds: vault write auth/kubernetes/role/app bound_service_account_names=app bound_service_account_namespaces=prod policies=app ttl=15m
tip: Trusted platform attestation turns who the workload is into the credential, which removes the chicken-and-egg problem.
a: The bootstrap problem is that to get secrets from a vault, an application first needs a credential for the vault, and storing that credential securely raises the same question again. The answer is to make the platform vouch for the workload. A cloud instance can present signed metadata, a Kubernetes pod presents its projected service account token, and CI presents an OIDC token. The secrets system verifies the signature, checks the claims against a configured role, and issues a short-lived token or credential in return. No long-lived password is ever placed into the image or configuration. Trust then relies on the integrity of the platform identity and on tight role bindings, such as namespace and service account name. Where hardware is involved, attestation with a TPM can prove the machine's identity. I also limit the lifetime and use count of the first token so a leak has little value.
f: What identities can the platform assert?

q: How do you handle certificate and key lifecycle with cert-manager and a private CA?
p: cert-manager automates issuance and renewal using Issuers backed by ACME, Vault or a private CA. Short-lived certs reduce exposure; monitor expiry, protect CA keys offline or in an HSM, and automate rotation end to end.
tip: Alert on certificates nearing expiry even when renewal is automated, because silent renewal failures cause outages.
a: Manual certificate handling leads to outages from expiry and to risk from long-lived private keys. cert-manager runs in the cluster, watches Certificate resources, requests certificates from a configured issuer, stores them as secrets and renews them before expiry. Issuers can be a public ACME service for ingress, Vault's PKI engine, or an internal certificate authority for service-to-service mTLS. I keep lifetimes short, days or weeks, so compromise has limited value and renewal becomes routine. The root CA key stays offline or in a hardware security module, and a protected intermediate signs workload certificates. I monitor the renewal status and set alerts on days to expiry, since webhook or quota problems can make renewal fail quietly. Applications must reload certificates without restart, or be restarted by a controller. Revocation is handled mostly by short lifetime rather than CRL distribution.
f: How do apps pick up renewed certs?

q: What is the OpenSSF Scorecard and how do you use it to evaluate dependencies?
p: Scorecard runs automated checks on open source projects, such as branch protection, code review, pinned dependencies, signed releases and vulnerability handling, producing a score. Use it as one signal when selecting and monitoring dependencies.
tip: A low score is a prompt to investigate, not an automatic ban. Combine with maintenance activity and usage context.
a: Choosing a dependency means trusting its maintainers and their practices. The Scorecard project automates a set of checks on the repository: whether the default branch is protected, whether changes need review, whether dependencies and workflows are pinned, whether releases are signed, whether there is a security policy, how recently it was maintained, and whether fuzzing or static analysis is used. Each check gets a score and there is an aggregate. I use it in two places. When evaluating a new library, a very low score on review and branch protection tells me that a single compromised account could ship malicious code. And in continuous monitoring, I scan the dependencies I already use and track trends. It is a heuristic, so I combine it with other evidence such as the bus factor, release cadence, known advisories and how critical the component is. For critical dependencies I may fork, vendor or sponsor maintenance.
f: What would a low Pinned-Dependencies score mean?
Does a high score guarantee safety?

q: How do you pin GitHub Actions and other CI dependencies to resist tag hijacking?
p: Pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs rather than mutable tags or branches, review updates through automated PRs, restrict allowed actions, and use minimal token permissions.
tip: Tags can be moved by an attacker who compromises the action repository. A commit SHA is immutable.
a: A workflow step that uses an action by tag trusts whatever that tag points to at run time. If the action's repository is compromised, an attacker can move the tag to a malicious commit, and every pipeline using it runs the attacker's code with access to the job's secrets and token, which actually happened in real incidents. Pinning to a full commit hash makes the reference immutable. To keep pins current without manual effort, I use a dependency bot that proposes updates as pull requests with a diff and release notes, so a human reviews each change. I also restrict the organisation to an allowlist of approved actions, set the default token permissions to read-only and grant write scopes per job, avoid running untrusted pull request code with secrets, and prefer well-known maintainers or vendoring small actions. The same principle applies to container images referenced by digest and scripts downloaded in pipelines.
f: How do you keep pins up to date?

q: How do you generate and consume an SBOM in a CI pipeline, and what formats exist?
p: Generate an SBOM per build with tools like Syft in SPDX or CycloneDX format, attach it to the image as an attestation, store it, and scan it continuously against new vulnerability data.
tip: The value is in re-scanning stored SBOMs when a new CVE drops, so you can answer 'where are we affected' in minutes.
a: A software bill of materials lists the components inside an artifact. In the pipeline I generate it right after building the image, using a scanner that inspects the packages in the final image and the language lockfiles, and output it in a standard format, either SPDX or CycloneDX. I then attach it to the image digest as a signed attestation, so consumers can verify it came from my pipeline, and also store it in a central inventory. The practical use comes later: when a new vulnerability such as a major library CVE is published, I query the stored SBOMs to find every affected service in minutes rather than scanning all repositories, and I can feed the same SBOMs to a vulnerability scanner on a schedule. Quality matters, so I check that the SBOM covers transitive dependencies and OS packages, and compare against what is actually deployed.
f: Why attach the SBOM to the digest?

q: What are reproducible builds and why do they matter for supply-chain security?
p: A reproducible build yields bit-for-bit identical output from the same source, so independent parties can verify that a binary matches its claimed source and detect tampering in the build environment.
tip: Common blockers are timestamps, file ordering, embedded paths and non-pinned dependencies.
a: The central trust question for a binary is whether it really came from the source code claimed. If builds are reproducible, two independent builders using the same source and toolchain produce identical bytes, so I can rebuild and compare hashes. A mismatch reveals a compromised build machine or a tampered artifact. Achieving it requires removing nondeterminism: embedding the commit time rather than the current time, sorting file lists, normalising paths and user IDs, pinning every dependency and the compiler version, and building in a clean, hermetic environment. Tools such as diffoscope show where two outputs differ. Even where fully bit-identical builds are impractical, hermetic and provenance-recording builds give much of the benefit. Reproducibility complements signing and provenance: signatures prove who built it, reproducibility lets others check that what they built was honest. Organisations often apply it first to their most critical or widely distributed components.

q: How do you secure a private package registry and prevent typosquatting and malicious packages?
p: Proxy public registries through an internal repository manager, allowlist packages, scope private namespaces, add cooldown periods and malware scanning, require lockfiles and integrity hashes, and block install scripts where possible.
tip: Install scripts execute with developer or CI privileges at install time, so treat new packages like running unknown code.
a: Developers and pipelines install code from the internet constantly, and attackers exploit that with typosquatted names, dependency confusion and compromised maintainers. I route all installs through an internal repository manager that proxies the public registry, so I have a single control point. There I can allow only approved or scanned packages, quarantine brand-new versions for a few days so that malicious releases are usually detected before they are consumed, and scan for known malware and vulnerabilities. Private package names are scoped to a namespace bound to the internal registry so a public package of the same name cannot win. Lockfiles with integrity hashes make installs deterministic and detect modification. I disable lifecycle install scripts by default and enable them case by case, and verify provenance and signatures where the ecosystem supports them. Developer education on checking package names also helps.

q: How do you assess and respond to a compromised maintainer or malicious release of a dependency you use?
p: Identify exposure through SBOMs and lockfiles, pin or roll back to a known good version, rotate any secrets exposed to affected builds, check for indicators of compromise, and block the version at the registry proxy.
tip: If the bad version ran in CI, assume that job's secrets were exposed and rotate them.
a: The first step is scoping: which of our services and build jobs used the affected version, and when. SBOMs and lockfiles answer that quickly, and the registry proxy logs show who downloaded it. I then contain: block the version in the internal registry, pin or roll back to the last known good release, rebuild and redeploy affected services. Next I assume impact where the package executed, since a malicious install script or runtime payload could have stolen environment variables, tokens or SSH keys, so I rotate any credential available to those CI jobs or hosts and review audit logs for misuse. I look for indicators of compromise published by researchers, such as network connections or files. Finally I communicate to teams, record a timeline, and improve controls such as version cooldowns, pinning by hash, install script restrictions and egress filtering from build runners.
f: How does the registry proxy help response?

q: What is in-toto and how does it add verifiable steps to a software supply chain?
p: in-toto defines a layout of required steps and who may perform them, and each step emits signed link metadata. A verifier checks that every step happened, by the right party, with matching materials and products.
cmds: in-toto-run --step-name build --key builder.key --materials src/ --products dist/ -- make
tip: Think of it as a signed checklist across the pipeline, so a skipped scan or an unauthorised build step is detectable.
a: Signing the final artifact only proves who signed it, not that the right process produced it. In-toto addresses this by describing the whole pipeline. The project owner defines a layout: the steps that must occur, such as code review, build, test and scan, which functionaries are authorised to perform each step, and the expected relationships between inputs and outputs. When each step runs, the tool records the materials consumed and products created with their hashes and signs this as link metadata. Before deployment, a verifier checks the layout's signature, confirms every required step has links signed by authorised keys, and that the products of one step match the materials of the next, so nothing was swapped between stages. The attestation concept in SLSA provenance and sigstore builds on the same idea. It makes bypassing a control, like skipping tests, cryptographically visible.
f: How is this different from signing the image?

q: How do you vet container base images and maintain an internal golden image pipeline?
p: Choose minimal, maintained bases, build golden images centrally with patching, scanning and signing, publish by digest, and rebuild on a schedule and on CVE triggers. Teams must use the approved images.
tip: Distroless or minimal images shrink the attack surface and the noise from scanners.
a: Every application image inherits the risk of its base, so I standardise a small set of approved bases. A platform team builds these golden images from minimal parents, such as distroless or a slim distribution, applies updates, removes shells and package managers where possible, adds only needed CA certificates and a non-root user, then scans and signs the result. They are rebuilt on a fixed schedule, for example weekly, and immediately when a critical vulnerability appears in a base package, then published with immutable digests. Application teams reference the base by digest through an automated update bot, so they get a pull request when a new base appears. An admission policy or registry rule ensures only images derived from approved bases run in production. Metrics track the age of bases in use, which shows teams lagging behind patches.
f: How do you enforce use of golden images?

q: How do you verify provenance of third-party binaries and tools downloaded in pipelines?
p: Pin versions, verify checksums and signatures from a trusted source, prefer package managers with verification, mirror approved tools internally, and avoid piping curl to bash.
tip: A checksum fetched from the same place as the binary only proves integrity in transit, not authenticity. Verify a signature.
a: Pipelines often download CLI tools and scripts, and a curl-to-shell pattern executes whatever the server returns that day. I pin exact versions and verify what I download. A checksum is the minimum, but if it comes from the same server as the binary an attacker who controls the server controls both, so I prefer cryptographic signatures verified against a key or identity I trust, such as a project's signing key or a sigstore identity. For the tools my builds depend on heavily, I mirror them into an internal artifact repository after verification, so pipelines pull the vetted copy and are not affected by upstream outages or tampering. Package manager installs with signature checks are better than ad hoc downloads. In build images I bake the verified tools into the image rather than downloading at run time. Egress filtering on runners limits unexpected downloads.
f: Why is a same-origin checksum weak?

q: How do you use Pod Security Standards with namespace labels and exemptions in practice?
p: Label namespaces with enforce, audit and warn levels (privileged, baseline, restricted). Start with warn and audit to find violations, fix workloads, then enforce. Exempt only specific system namespaces or users.
tip: The server-side dry-run label shows which existing pods would violate a level before you enforce it.
a: Pod Security Admission is the built-in replacement for pod security policies. It applies one of three standards per namespace through labels: privileged, baseline, which blocks known escalations, and restricted, which follows current hardening practice such as non-root, dropped capabilities and a seccomp profile. Each namespace can have separate modes: enforce rejects violating pods, audit records violations in the audit log, and warn returns warnings to the user. My rollout is gradual. I first add audit and warn labels at the target level, and use the server-side dry-run to see which existing workloads would fail. Teams fix manifests, then I enable enforce, starting with restricted for application namespaces and baseline or privileged only for system components that truly need it. Exemptions in the admission configuration are kept minimal and documented. For finer rules than the three levels, I add policy engines such as Kyverno.
f: How do you test before enforcing?

q: What is a securityContext and which settings give the best hardening for a typical application pod?
p: runAsNonRoot, a numeric UID, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation false, drop ALL capabilities, seccompProfile RuntimeDefault, and no hostPath or host namespaces. Mount writable emptyDirs only where needed.
cmds: securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 10001 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
tip: Test with the restricted Pod Security level. If your manifest passes it, you have the main hardening in place.
a: The securityContext defines the privileges the container process has. A strong baseline for ordinary applications is: run as a non-root numeric user, so the process cannot write to root-owned locations or bind privileged ports; disable privilege escalation so setuid binaries cannot raise privileges; drop all Linux capabilities and add back only specific ones if truly required; make the root filesystem read-only and provide emptyDir volumes only for paths that must be writable; and apply the runtime default seccomp profile to filter dangerous system calls. Also avoid privileged mode, host networking, host PID and hostPath mounts. These settings limit what an attacker can do after exploiting the application, and they reduce container escape opportunities. Some images assume root or writable paths, so I fix them at build time. Admission policies enforce the baseline across all teams.

q: How do you audit and reduce excessive Kubernetes RBAC permissions?
p: Review bindings with tools such as kubectl-who-can, rbac-tool and audit logs, remove cluster-admin and wildcard grants, prefer namespaced Roles, avoid access to secrets and exec, and generate least-privilege roles from observed usage.
cmds: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .subjects'
tip: Access to create pods, read secrets, or exec into pods is effectively privilege escalation, so treat those verbs as sensitive.
a: Over-permissive RBAC is one of the most common Kubernetes risks. I start with an inventory: list cluster role bindings, particularly any that grant cluster-admin, wildcard resources or verbs, and bindings to broad groups. For each service account I ask what it can actually do, using the can-i listing and who-can plugins. Certain verbs are dangerous even when they look benign: read access to secrets, the ability to create pods which can mount anything, exec into pods, impersonation, and the rights to modify roles or bindings, which enables escalation. To right-size, I compare granted permissions against the API calls actually seen in audit logs, and generate narrower namespaced roles. Human access goes through the identity provider with groups, and break-glass admin is time-limited. I review regularly and add policy that blocks wildcard roles from being created.
f: How do audit logs help right-size roles?

q: How do you secure the container runtime with gVisor, Kata Containers or user namespaces for untrusted workloads?
p: Sandboxed runtimes add a boundary between workload and host kernel: gVisor intercepts syscalls in user space, Kata runs pods in lightweight VMs, user namespaces map root in the container to an unprivileged host user. Use via RuntimeClass.
tip: Sandboxing trades some performance and compatibility for a stronger isolation boundary. Apply it where tenants are untrusted.
a: Standard containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability can allow an escape. For untrusted or multi-tenant workloads, such as running customer code or build jobs, I add isolation. gVisor implements a user-space kernel that intercepts and handles most system calls, greatly reducing the attack surface exposed to the host kernel. Kata Containers runs each pod inside a lightweight virtual machine with its own kernel, giving hardware-virtualisation isolation. Both are selected per pod through a RuntimeClass, so I can sandbox only the risky workloads. User namespaces are another layer: root inside the container maps to an unprivileged user on the host, so even a breakout has limited rights. The costs are overhead, startup time and incomplete syscall or device support, so I benchmark and test compatibility, and combine sandboxing with network policy, minimal permissions and node isolation.
f: How do you select a sandbox for a pod?

q: How do you protect Kubernetes nodes with hardened OS images, minimal access and kubelet settings?
p: Use minimal immutable node OS images, disable SSH, restrict kubelet anonymous access and read-only port, enable authorization webhook mode, apply patches by replacing nodes, and monitor with runtime tools.
tip: Test that the kubelet port rejects unauthenticated requests. An open kubelet API means remote command execution on pods.
a: Worker nodes run my workloads and hold credentials, so a compromised node is a serious event. I use minimal, purpose-built node operating systems with an immutable root filesystem and automatic replacement rather than in-place patching, so drift and manual changes are eliminated. SSH access is disabled in favour of audited session tooling, and nodes sit in private subnets. The kubelet is configured with anonymous authentication off, authorization mode set to webhook so the API server decides, the read-only port disabled, and rotation of its certificates enabled. I benchmark against the CIS guidelines with tools like kube-bench. The cloud metadata endpoint is protected so pods cannot obtain the node's credentials, and nodes have only the minimum cloud permissions. Runtime detection watches for shells, unexpected network connections and file changes. Patching means rolling out a new image and draining old nodes.
f: Why replace nodes instead of patching?

q: How do you secure etcd, including encryption at rest, access control and backups?
p: Restrict etcd to the API server with mTLS, isolate network access, enable encryption of Secrets at rest using a KMS provider, encrypt and access-control backups, and monitor access. Managed control planes handle much of this.
cmds: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --cacert ca.crt --cert client.crt --key client.key endpoint health
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1 kind: EncryptionConfiguration resources: - resources: [secrets] providers: [kms: {name: kms, endpoint: unix:///kms.sock}]
tip: Base64 in a Secret is not encryption. Without encryption at rest, anyone with etcd or backup access reads every secret.
a: etcd stores all cluster state, including Secrets, so access to it is equivalent to full cluster control. Only the API server should talk to it, over mutually authenticated TLS, with network rules that block everything else, and its peer traffic encrypted too. Kubernetes Secrets are stored base64 encoded, which is not protection, so I enable encryption at rest in the API server, ideally with an envelope scheme where a key management service holds the master key, so the data on disk and in snapshots is ciphertext. Backups are encrypted, stored with restricted access, tested for restore, and retention is limited. I audit who accesses etcd and the API, and rotate keys periodically. In managed services like EKS, GKE and AKS the provider operates etcd, but I still enable the available secrets encryption option with my own key to meet compliance and keep control.
f: What is envelope encryption for secrets?

q: What is Kubernetes audit logging, and how do you design an audit policy that is useful without being overwhelming?
p: Audit logs record API requests by who, what and when. A policy sets levels (None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse) by resource. Log secrets at Metadata only, log writes in detail, drop noisy reads, and ship logs to a SIEM.
tip: Never log request bodies for secrets, or the audit log itself becomes a store of secrets.
a: Audit logging answers who did what to which resource and when, which is essential for incident investigation and compliance. Each API request generates events through stages, and the audit policy decides how much to record per rule. The levels range from none, through metadata only, to the request body, to request and response bodies. Recording everything at the highest level would be huge and could capture sensitive data, so I design the policy deliberately. I drop high-volume noise like health checks and routine get and watch calls from system components, log secrets and config maps at metadata level only, and record full request bodies for sensitive changes such as RBAC modifications, pod creation, exec and port-forward, and admission webhook changes. The logs are shipped off the node to a SIEM with retention, and detection rules alert on suspicious patterns like exec into production pods or role binding changes.
f: Why not log secrets at RequestResponse?

q: How do you secure ingress and API gateways, including TLS, WAF integration and rate limiting?
p: Terminate TLS with modern settings and managed certificates, enforce HTTPS and HSTS, add a WAF, rate-limit and authenticate at the edge, restrict admin paths, and keep ingress controllers patched and isolated.
tip: The ingress controller is internet-facing and highly privileged, so treat it as critical, patch quickly, and limit its RBAC.
a: Ingress is the front door of the cluster, so hardening it has high value. At the transport layer I terminate TLS with current protocol versions and strong ciphers, automate certificates, redirect HTTP to HTTPS and send HSTS. In front of or alongside the controller, a web application firewall filters common attacks, and I configure rate limits and connection limits per client to blunt brute force and denial of service. The gateway can enforce authentication, such as validating JWTs or client certificates, before traffic reaches services. Admin or internal paths are not exposed publicly. The controller itself runs with minimal permissions, since it often can read secrets across namespaces, in a dedicated namespace with network policy, and it is patched promptly because vulnerabilities in popular controllers are actively exploited. Configuration snippets from users are restricted via admission policy to avoid injection.
f: Why is the ingress controller high risk?

q: How do you handle image pull secrets and registry authentication securely in Kubernetes?
p: Use workload or node identity for cloud registries to avoid static pull secrets, scope credentials read-only per registry, rotate them, and attach pull secrets to service accounts rather than each pod.
tip: With cloud registries, node or workload IAM roles remove the need to store pull credentials in the cluster at all.
a: Pulling private images requires credentials, and static registry passwords stored as Kubernetes secrets are long-lived and widely readable. On cloud platforms I avoid them: the node or workload identity is granted read-only pull permission on the registry, and the kubelet obtains short-lived tokens through a credential provider. Where a static credential is unavoidable, for a third-party registry, I create a dedicated read-only robot account scoped to specific repositories, store it through the secrets management flow, and rotate it. Rather than adding the pull secret to every pod spec, I attach it to the service account in each namespace, so it is applied consistently. I use pull-through caches to limit exposure to public registries and rate limits. Namespaces have RBAC that prevents unrelated teams reading the secret, and policy forces images to come from approved registries only.

q: How do you write and test Rego policies with conftest and OPA unit tests?
p: Write policies as deny rules over structured input, test them with opa test using fixtures for allowed and denied cases, and run conftest in CI against manifests or Terraform plan JSON. Include messages that explain the fix.
cmds: deny[msg] { input.kind == "Deployment"; not input.spec.template.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot; msg := "pods must run as non-root" }
tip: Test both the denied and allowed paths, and include edge cases like missing fields, because Rego treats undefined as false.
a: Rego is declarative, so I think in terms of rules that produce violation messages when conditions hold. I write each policy in its own file with a clear message that tells the developer how to fix the problem, not only what is wrong. For example, a rule that denies a deployment when the pod security context does not set run as non-root. I test policies like code: unit tests with the OPA test command feed sample inputs and assert that violations appear exactly when expected, including the passing case and edge cases such as missing fields, because an undefined value in Rego makes a rule silently not fire. In pipelines, conftest evaluates policies against Kubernetes manifests, Helm output or Terraform plan JSON, failing the build on violations. Policies live in a versioned repository with review, release tags and a documented exception mechanism, and I measure how often rules block changes to tune them.

q: What is Kyverno's verifyImages and how does it enforce signed images?
p: verifyImages is a Kyverno rule type that checks image signatures or attestations at admission, using cosign keys or keyless identities, and can mutate tags to digests. Unverified images are rejected.
cmds: verifyImages: - imageReferences: ["registry.example.com/*"] attestors: - entries: - keyless: { issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com", subject: "https://github.com/acme/*" }
tip: Verify against an identity (who built it), not just that some signature exists. Any attacker can sign with their own key.
a: Image signing is only useful if something checks it at deploy time. Kyverno's verifyImages rule does that inside the admission webhook. For images matching a registry pattern, it verifies the signature using either a static public key or keyless verification, where the policy states which identity provider issuer and which subject, such as a particular repository's release workflow, are acceptable. It can also check attached attestations, such as a vulnerability scan result or provenance, and require specific fields. A helpful side effect is that the rule can rewrite mutable tags to the immutable digest that was verified, preventing a swap between verification and pull. I roll the policy out in audit mode first to see what would fail, then enforce. Exceptions for system images are explicit, and the key or identity configuration is managed through GitOps and rotated carefully.
f: Why verify identity, not just a signature?
What does rewriting to a digest prevent?

q: How do you use ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and CEL as a native alternative to webhook-based policy engines?
p: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy lets the API server evaluate CEL expressions in-process, so no external webhook is needed. It is fast, reliable and simple for common checks, with bindings selecting where to apply.
cmds: validations: - expression: "object.spec.replicas <= 10" message: "replicas must be 10 or fewer"
tip: No webhook means no availability dependency and no extra latency, but CEL has less power than Rego for complex logic.
a: Webhook-based policy engines add moving parts: a service that must be available, with latency and failure policy decisions. Kubernetes now offers validating admission policies, where rules are written as expressions in the common expression language and evaluated inside the API server itself. A policy resource defines the matching resources and the expressions that must be true, with messages for failure, and a separate binding says which namespaces or objects it applies to and whether to deny, warn or audit. Because evaluation is in-process there is no network hop, no outage risk from a webhook, and strong performance. It works well for straightforward constraints such as replica limits, required labels, forbidding hostPath or privileged containers. For richer needs such as mutation, generation, external data lookups, image verification or cross-resource logic, a policy engine like Kyverno or Gatekeeper remains useful, and they can be combined.
f: What are the limits of CEL?

q: How do you build a policy exception process that is auditable and time-bound?
p: Exceptions are requested as code, linked to a ticket and owner, approved by security, scoped narrowly, and given an expiry. Dashboards track active exceptions, and automation removes or flags expired ones.
cmds: apiVersion: kyverno.io/v2 kind: PolicyException metadata: { name: legacy-root, annotations: { expires: "2026-12-31", ticket: "SEC-1042" } }
kubectl get policyexception -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations.expires < "2026-10-21")'
tip: An exception without an expiry becomes permanent policy. Make the default end date short.
a: Rigid policy without exceptions gets bypassed, while unmanaged exceptions erode security. I make exceptions a first-class, reviewable object. A team opens a request describing the workload, the rule, the reason, the compensating controls and the owner. If approved, the exception is committed as code in a dedicated repository, using the policy engine's exception resource, scoped as narrowly as possible, for example one deployment in one namespace rather than a whole cluster. Each has an expiry date and a ticket reference. Automation lists active exceptions on a dashboard, notifies owners before expiry, and either removes the exception or opens a review when time is up. Metrics show the number of exceptions per policy, which tells me when a rule is unrealistic and should be changed. Because everything is in Git, the audit trail shows who approved what and when.
f: What do exception counts tell you?

q: How do you scan Helm charts and Kubernetes manifests in CI with kube-linter, kubesec, Trivy and Checkov?
p: Render charts to manifests, then run linters and scanners for misconfigurations such as privileged pods, missing limits and latest tags. Fail on high severity, report the rest, and keep rules consistent with admission policy.
tip: Scan the rendered output with production values, since misconfigurations often come from values files, not the chart defaults.
a: Static analysis of manifests catches risky configuration before it reaches a cluster. For Helm, I render the chart with the real values file for each environment, because settings that matter, like security contexts or image tags, are often set through values. The rendered YAML goes through several tools: a linter that looks for best practice violations such as missing resource limits, probes or the latest tag, a misconfiguration scanner that flags privileged containers, host namespaces, and dangerous capabilities, and optionally a policy check with the same Rego or Kyverno rules used at admission, so developers see failures in the pull request instead of at deploy time. I set severity thresholds: high and critical findings fail the build, lower ones are reported. Findings link to documentation on how to fix, and suppressions require justification in code. Periodic scans of live clusters catch drift.
f: Why align CI rules with admission rules?

q: What is the difference between preventive, detective and corrective controls in policy as code?
p: Preventive controls block bad changes (admission, CI gates, SCPs), detective controls find issues after the fact (CSPM, audits, drift detection), corrective controls fix automatically or via remediation workflow. Mature programs layer all three.
tip: Preventive controls are cheapest per incident, but detective ones are needed for what you could not or did not prevent.
a: These describe where in time a control acts. Preventive controls stop non-compliant changes from happening: admission policies that reject a privileged pod, CI checks that fail a build, or organisation-level guardrails that deny creating a public bucket. Detective controls observe the state afterwards and report deviations, such as posture management scanning cloud accounts, config rules evaluating resources, drift detection, and audit-mode policies. They are essential because not every path is covered by prevention, and because old resources predate the rules. Corrective controls respond: an automation that removes a public ACL, quarantines a pod, or opens a ticket with an SLA for the owning team. A strong program layers them. I start with detection to learn the baseline, move high-confidence rules to prevention, and automate correction for well-understood cases while keeping humans in the loop for risky ones.
f: Why do you need detective controls too?

q: How do you enforce tagging, ownership and cost-allocation standards through policy?
p: Define required tags, enforce on creation via IaC policy checks and cloud tag policies or SCPs, detect gaps with scanning, and tie tags to ownership for alerts and cost reports. Inherit tags automatically where possible.
cmds: aws organizations create-policy --type TAG_POLICY --name required-tags --content file://tags.json
az policy assignment create --name require-owner --policy 'Require a tag on resources'
tip: Tags let a security finding find its owner. An unowned resource is an unfixed finding.
a: Consistent metadata makes security and finance operations work: when a scanner finds an exposed bucket, the owner tag tells me who to contact, and cost reports depend on allocation tags. I define a small mandatory set, such as owner team, environment, service and cost centre, with allowed values. Enforcement happens at several layers. In pull requests, plan checks written in Rego fail if a resource lacks required tags. In the cloud, tag policies and organisation guardrails can reject creation of untagged resources or standardise formats, and modules inject default tags so developers rarely forget. For existing resources, scheduled queries find gaps and report them by team. Some tags can be inherited from the account or resource group. The result is that every finding and every dollar maps to an accountable owner, and dashboards show compliance percentage, which creates healthy pressure to fix it.
f: Why do tags matter for security?

q: How do you use AWS Organizations SCPs, Azure Policy and GCP organisation policies as preventive guardrails?
p: They set boundaries above individual accounts or projects: deny dangerous actions, restrict regions and services, require encryption. They limit what even admins can do inside, and complement IAM rather than replace it.
tip: Guardrails set the maximum permissions, they don't grant any. Test them in a sandbox OU first because a bad deny can break pipelines.
a: Identity policies grant permissions to principals, but a single misconfigured admin can still do anything within an account. Organisation-level guardrails sit above and define what is impossible regardless of IAM. In AWS, service control policies attached to organisational units deny actions such as disabling CloudTrail, leaving the organisation, using unapproved regions, or creating unencrypted volumes. Azure Policy assigns rules at management group or subscription level, to deny, audit or automatically remediate resources. Google organisation policies apply constraints like disabling service account key creation or restricting public IPs. I apply them through a landing zone design with environments separated into different OUs, start in audit or in a sandbox, then enforce, with a documented exception process. They don't grant access, only limit it, so effective permission is the intersection of the guardrail and the identity policy.
f: How do you roll out a new deny safely?

q: How do you secure serverless and managed container platforms (Lambda, Cloud Run, Fargate) differently from VMs?
p: The provider secures the host, so focus shifts to code, dependencies, per-function IAM roles, secrets handling, event input validation, network egress controls and logging. Use least privilege per function and short timeouts.
tip: One shared over-privileged role for all functions is the classic serverless mistake. Give each function its own scoped role.
a: With serverless and managed containers, the provider handles patching of the operating system and runtime isolation, so my responsibility moves up the stack. I focus on identity: each function or service gets its own role with only the permissions it needs, because one compromised function with broad rights becomes a pivot to the account. Input is the main attack surface, since events from queues, buckets and APIs may carry attacker-controlled data, so I validate and treat all event fields as untrusted to prevent injection. Dependencies are scanned, since the package contents are my code. Secrets come from a secrets manager at runtime rather than environment variables in the template. I limit network egress with private connectivity and restrict outbound access, set reasonable timeouts and concurrency limits to contain abuse and cost, enable structured logging and tracing, and use code signing or image verification for deployment integrity.
f: What is the attack surface of an event-driven function?

q: How do you use IAM Access Analyzer, Policy Sentinel-style tools or CIEM to find unused and external access?
p: Analyzers find resources shared outside the account or organisation and permissions unused over a period, and generate least-privilege policies from CloudTrail activity. Run continuously and route findings to owners.
tip: Unused permissions and unused roles are free attack surface. Remove them on a schedule.
a: Over time, cloud permissions accumulate far beyond what workloads use. Analyzer tools help in two ways. External access analysis reasons about resource policies and tells me which buckets, roles, keys or queues can be reached from outside my account or organisation, which finds accidental sharing. Unused access analysis compares granted permissions with actual activity from audit logs and reports roles, keys and permissions that haven't been used for, say, ninety days. Policy generation goes further, producing a least-privilege policy from observed behaviour that I review and apply. Cloud infrastructure entitlement management products extend this across multiple clouds. I run these continuously, send findings to owners with severity and SLA, and automate cleanup where safe, such as disabling long-unused access keys. Reviews combine tooling output with human judgement, since rarely used break-glass permissions should remain.
f: What does external access analysis find?
How do you handle rarely used break-glass roles?

q: How do you design and secure cross-account access in AWS using roles and external IDs?
p: Use IAM roles assumed via sts:AssumeRole, with trust policies naming exact principals, conditions such as MFA or source organisation, and external IDs for third parties to prevent confused deputy attacks. Avoid long-lived user keys.
tip: The external ID stops a third party from being tricked into using their access to your account on someone else's behalf.
a: Instead of sharing credentials between accounts, I create a role in the target account whose trust policy names which principals in other accounts may assume it. Callers request temporary credentials and their activity is logged against the session. To tighten the trust, I specify exact roles rather than a whole account root where possible, add conditions requiring multi-factor authentication for human access, and restrict to principals in my own organisation using the organisation ID condition key. When granting access to a third-party vendor, an external ID adds protection against the confused deputy problem: the vendor, who serves many customers, must present the unique ID I gave them, so another customer cannot trick the vendor's system into acting on my account. Permissions on the role are least privilege, session duration is short, and CloudTrail events from role assumption are monitored for unusual sources or times.
f: What is the confused deputy problem?

q: How do you secure DNS and prevent subdomain takeover?
p: Inventory DNS records, remove dangling CNAMEs pointing to deprovisioned cloud resources, monitor for them continuously, use DNSSEC and registrar locks, and tie DNS changes to resource lifecycle in IaC.
tip: Delete the DNS record in the same change that deletes the cloud resource it points to.
a: A subdomain takeover happens when a DNS record still points to a cloud service resource that has been deleted, such as a storage website, a PaaS app or a CDN endpoint, and an attacker claims the same name on that service. They then serve content on my trusted domain, enabling phishing, cookie theft or malware delivery. Prevention is lifecycle discipline: create and remove DNS records in the same infrastructure as code that manages the resource, so deleting one deletes the other. Detection is continuous: enumerate all records, resolve them, and flag CNAMEs that point to services returning a not-found or unclaimed error. Many clouds support domain verification, so a claim requires proving ownership of the domain. I also protect the registrar account with strong authentication and a registry lock, enable DNSSEC where appropriate, and limit who can change zones with audited access.
f: How does an attacker claim the resource?
Why manage DNS in the same IaC?

q: How do you build a cloud incident response capability with forensic snapshots, isolation and log preservation?
p: Prepare in advance: centralised immutable logs, a dedicated forensics account, runbooks, and automation to isolate (quarantine security group, disable keys), snapshot disks and memory, and preserve evidence with chain of custody.
cmds: aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id AKIA... --status Inactive --user-name suspect
tip: Isolate, don't terminate. Terminating a compromised instance destroys memory and volatile evidence.
a: Good incident response in the cloud depends on preparation. Logs from audit trails, network flows and application sources go to a separate, write-protected account with retention, so an attacker in a workload account cannot erase them. I keep runbooks and automation ready for common cases. For a suspect instance, the first move is containment by replacing its security groups with a quarantine group that blocks traffic but leaves it running, and revoking or disabling any credentials it holds, rather than deleting it. Then I capture evidence: snapshot the volumes, take a memory image if tooling exists, and copy the data into a locked forensic account with object lock, recording hashes and who handled what for chain of custody. Analysis happens on copies in an isolated environment. Afterwards I eradicate, rebuild from clean images, rotate credentials, and write a post-incident review with improvements.

q: How do you handle authentication and session security with OAuth2, OIDC and JWT correctly?
p: Use authorization code flow with PKCE, validate issuer, audience, signature and expiry, keep tokens short-lived with refresh rotation, store them safely, and never put sensitive data in unencrypted JWTs.
cmds: code_challenge=$(echo -n $VERIFIER | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')
tip: Reject tokens with alg none and pin accepted algorithms. Never trust the header to choose verification behaviour.
a: OAuth2 handles delegated authorisation and OpenID Connect adds identity on top. For browser and mobile apps I use the authorization code flow with PKCE, which prevents interception of the code, and avoid the implicit flow. When my API receives a JWT access token, I must validate it fully: verify the signature against the issuer's published keys, check the issuer and audience claims match my service, check expiry and not-before times, and confirm required scopes. I pin the allowed signing algorithms to avoid algorithm confusion attacks, including the none algorithm. Access tokens are short-lived, and refresh tokens rotate with reuse detection so a stolen refresh token is noticed. Tokens are stored in secure, httpOnly cookies or platform secure storage rather than local storage where scripts can read them. JWT payloads are only encoded, not encrypted, so I do not put sensitive data in them, and I have a revocation strategy for compromised sessions.

q: How do you secure file uploads and prevent SSRF, path traversal and deserialization vulnerabilities?
p: For uploads: validate type by content, limit size, rename files, store outside the web root with no execute permission. For SSRF: allowlist destinations and block internal ranges. Avoid unsafe deserialization and canonicalise paths.
cmds: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/   # must be blocked from app pods
tip: Never trust the filename or Content-Type header from a client. Both are attacker-controlled.
a: These are three separate classes with a shared root cause: trusting input that the attacker controls. For file uploads I check the real content type rather than the extension or header, limit size, generate a random server-side name, store files in object storage or a directory outside the web root with execution disabled, and scan for malware. Path traversal is prevented by never concatenating user input into file paths; I resolve the final path and verify it stays within the intended base directory. Server-side request forgery occurs when the app fetches a user-supplied URL, so I use an allowlist of hosts, resolve DNS and block private, loopback and link-local addresses including the cloud metadata address, disable redirects or revalidate them, and enforce metadata service v2 style protections. For deserialization I avoid native object formats for untrusted data and use simple data formats with schema validation.

q: What is software composition analysis and how do you prioritise findings beyond CVSS scores?
p: SCA finds known vulnerabilities in dependencies. Prioritise by reachability, exploit availability (EPSS, KEV), exposure of the service, data sensitivity and fix availability, not CVSS alone.
tip: CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities list is a strong signal that a CVE is being used in attacks right now.
a: Software composition analysis compares the libraries in my code against vulnerability databases. Raw output can be thousands of findings, many irrelevant, so prioritisation is the real work. CVSS describes severity in theory but not likelihood. I add several signals: is a public exploit available and is it being exploited in the wild, as shown by the known exploited list and the exploit prediction score; is the vulnerable function actually reachable from my code, which reachability analysis can estimate; is the service internet-facing or internal; what data does it handle; and is a fixed version available. A high CVSS in a test-only dependency matters less than a medium one in a public authentication service. I set SLAs by combined risk, automate fix pull requests, suppress findings with documented not-affected statements using VEX, and track time to remediate as a metric.

q: How do you perform threat modeling with STRIDE on a new feature, and make it lightweight for agile teams?
p: Draw a data flow diagram, mark trust boundaries, apply STRIDE (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege) to each element, record mitigations and track them as tickets. Keep sessions short and recurring.
cmds: gh issue create --title 'Mitigate: JWT replay on /refresh' --label threat-model
tip: Focus on trust boundaries. The interesting threats are where data crosses from one trust level to another.
a: Threat modeling is structured thinking about what can go wrong before code is written. For a new feature I sketch a simple data flow diagram showing actors, services, data stores and flows, and draw the trust boundaries, such as internet to service or service to database. Then for each element and flow I walk through STRIDE: can someone spoof an identity, tamper with data, deny having done something, disclose information, disrupt availability, or elevate privileges. Each plausible threat gets a mitigation, an accepted-risk decision, or a follow-up ticket, with an owner. To keep it agile, I time-box sessions to under an hour with developers present, reuse templates and previous models, trigger it only for changes that alter data flows or trust boundaries, and store the model in the repository next to the code. The output feeds security test cases and acceptance criteria.
f: When do you trigger a new model?

q: How do you secure GraphQL and gRPC APIs differently from REST?
p: GraphQL needs query depth and complexity limits, introspection control, per-field authorisation and batching limits. gRPC needs mTLS, per-method authz, message size limits and reflection control. Both still need validation and rate limiting.
cmds: query { a { b { c { d } } } }   # depth attack
tip: GraphQL's single endpoint hides authorisation gaps. Check permissions per field and per object, not per URL.
a: The principles stay the same, but the attack surface shifts. GraphQL exposes one endpoint where clients shape queries, so a malicious client can craft deeply nested or expensive queries, or send many aliased operations in one request to bypass rate limits. I enforce limits on depth, complexity and batch size, set timeouts, and disable or restrict introspection in production. Authorisation cannot rely on URL paths, so resolvers check access for each object and field. Errors should not leak internals. For gRPC, which typically runs between services, I require mutual TLS, authenticate callers with tokens or workload identity, authorise per method, set maximum message sizes and deadlines, and turn off server reflection in production. For both, I still validate every input against the schema, apply rate limiting at the gateway, log sensible metadata and test with API-aware fuzzers.
f: How can aliasing bypass rate limits?

q: What are secure coding guardrails for AI-assisted or third-party generated code in the pipeline?
p: Treat generated or copied code as untrusted: run the same SAST, SCA, secret scanning and review as human code, require tests, restrict secrets exposure to tools, and check licences and provenance.
tip: The review burden shifts to verifying behaviour. Require tests and a human who understands the change before merge.
a: Code from an assistant, a snippet from the internet or a vendored sample can contain vulnerabilities, outdated APIs, hard-coded secrets, or licence obligations, and it can look convincing. The guardrail is that nothing bypasses the normal pipeline. It goes through pull request review by an engineer who actually understands the change, automated tests that exercise behaviour, static analysis for insecure patterns, dependency and licence scanning, and secret detection before commit and in CI. Developers must not paste confidential data or credentials into external tools, so I set policy and provide approved, access-controlled tooling. Any new dependency suggested must be vetted, since invented or typosquatted package names are a real risk. Where tools act with access to repositories or shells, I limit their permissions, run them in sandboxes, and log their actions. Metrics on defects and findings help calibrate the review level.

q: How do you implement rate limiting, bot protection and abuse prevention for public endpoints?
p: Apply layered limits at the edge and the application per IP, per user and per token, with token bucket algorithms, progressive challenges, anomaly detection, and returning 429 with Retry-After. Protect sensitive flows such as login and signup more tightly.
tip: Limit by identity (account, API key) as well as IP, since attackers rotate IPs and many legitimate users share one.
a: Public endpoints get abused by credential stuffing, scraping, enumeration and resource exhaustion. I use several layers. At the edge, a CDN or web application firewall provides coarse per-IP limits, managed bot detection and DDoS absorption. In the application or gateway, I apply finer limits keyed by authenticated user, API key or tenant, using algorithms like token bucket that allow short bursts but cap sustained rates, and return 429 with a retry hint. Sensitive flows such as login, password reset and sign-up get stricter limits, progressive delays, lockout with care to avoid enabling denial of service against real users, and challenges like CAPTCHA when risk is high. I add detection of anomalies: many failed logins across accounts, enumeration patterns, unusual user agents. Monitoring dashboards and alerts show spikes, and I review limits regularly against real traffic to avoid blocking customers.
f: Why not limit only by IP?
What are the risks of account lockout?

q: How do you map security controls to compliance frameworks like SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS without duplicating effort?
p: Build one control library, map each control to multiple framework requirements, automate evidence collection from systems, and run continuous control monitoring. Audit once, satisfy many.
cmds: steampipe query "select * from aws_s3_bucket where not versioning_enabled"
tip: Evidence from Git history, tickets and system configuration is stronger and cheaper than screenshots collected before the audit.
a: Frameworks overlap heavily: access control, change management, logging, encryption, vulnerability management and incident response appear in all of them in different words. So I define one internal control set, written in plain language, and map each control to the specific clauses of each framework in a matrix. Engineering implements the control once, for example required reviews for production changes, and the same evidence satisfies several requirements. The efficient part is automation of evidence: configuration queries, policy-as-code results, pull request approvals, vulnerability scan reports and access review exports are collected on a schedule and stored, so an audit samples live records rather than relying on screenshots gathered in a rush. Continuous control monitoring shows when a control drifts, and owners get alerts. Compliance is the minimum baseline; the real objective is actual risk reduction, and I avoid box-ticking controls that provide no security value.
f: What evidence is strongest for an auditor?
Why is compliance not equal to security?

q: How do you run effective access reviews and manage the joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle?
p: Automate provisioning from the HR system, use role-based groups, review privileged access frequently and general access periodically, remove access on moves and exits immediately, and keep evidence of reviewers' decisions.
cmds: aws iam generate-credential-report && aws iam get-credential-report
tip: Access that nobody reviews tends to grow forever. Make inactive access expire by default.
a: Access should follow roles that follow people's jobs. Joiners receive baseline access automatically through groups linked to the identity provider and HR record, with additional access requested and approved. Movers lose permissions of their old role as they gain the new one, which is where privilege creep usually starts. Leavers are deprovisioned immediately and completely, including SaaS accounts, API keys and cloud roles, ideally triggered by the HR event. Periodic access reviews ask managers or resource owners to confirm each person still needs their access; for privileged access I review monthly or quarterly, and for standard access less often. Review packets must be clear and prefilled with last-used data to help reviewers decide. Decisions and removals are recorded as audit evidence. I reduce workload by using time-limited, just-in-time elevation and by auto-expiring access that has been inactive.

q: How do you design a vulnerability management SLA policy and handle exceptions?
p: Set remediation deadlines by severity and exposure (for example critical internet-facing in days, low in quarter), measure compliance, require risk-accepted exceptions with owner, compensating controls and expiry, and escalate breaches.
cmds: trivy image --severity CRITICAL --format json app:1.4 | jq '.Results[].Vulnerabilities | length'
gh api repos/org/repo/dependabot/alerts -q '.[] | select(.state=="open") | .security_advisory.severity' | sort | uniq -c
tip: Track mean time to remediate and the percentage within SLA per team. Trends show whether the program is working.
a: A policy turns scattered patching into a managed process. I define target remediation times based on risk: critical vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems or those with known exploitation get a very short window, such as a few days; high severity gets a couple of weeks; medium and low are handled within regular maintenance cycles. Exposure and exploit information can adjust the deadline up or down. Findings flow automatically into the teams' backlogs with an owner. If a fix cannot be applied in time, the team requests an exception that states the reason, the compensating controls such as network isolation or a virtual patch, the risk owner who accepts it, and a firm expiry for re-evaluation. Reporting covers overdue counts, mean time to remediate and SLA compliance per team, reviewed regularly with engineering leadership, with escalation paths for repeated breaches.

q: How do you run a security champions program and embed security into engineering teams at scale?
p: Recruit volunteer engineers per team, give them training, tooling and a direct line to security, align incentives, share metrics, and make secure paths the easy default through paved roads and templates.
tip: Champions amplify the security team, but only if they get time allocated and recognition for the role.
a: A central security team cannot review everything, so I extend its reach through champions: one interested engineer in each product team who acts as the local point of contact. I give them structured training, access to tools and early information on new risks, regular community sessions, and time in their workload to do the job, and I recognise the contribution in performance conversations. Champions run threat modeling sessions, help triage scanner findings and review risky changes. Equally important is making the secure way the easy way: paved road templates, shared pipeline components with scanning built in, vetted libraries for authentication and encryption, and clear short guidance. I measure outcomes such as vulnerabilities found early, time to fix, and training participation, and share them transparently. The culture goal is that security is viewed as a quality attribute owned by engineering, with security acting as enabler.
f: What do champions need to succeed?

q: What is a security posture dashboard and which metrics should it show to executives and engineers?
p: Executives need risk trend, time to remediate critical issues, coverage, incident metrics and compliance status. Engineers need actionable per-service findings, SLA status and ownership. Avoid vanity counts.
tip: A single big number such as total vulnerabilities rewards the wrong behaviour. Show risk-weighted and trend-based metrics.
a: Different audiences need different views from the same data. For executives I show a small set of trends tied to risk: open critical and exploitable vulnerabilities and how fast they are closed, percentage of services covered by key controls such as scanning, MFA and logging, incident counts and detection and response times, and audit and compliance status. For engineering teams the dashboard is operational: findings grouped by service and owner with severity, age, SLA status and a link to the fix, so they can act without hunting. I avoid vanity metrics like total scans run or raw vulnerability count, which can rise simply because coverage improved, and prefer risk-weighted measures, mean time to remediate and the ratio of issues caught before production. Data comes from the scanners and cloud posture tools via a common pipeline, with consistent ownership tags, and each metric has a defined meaning and a target.

q: A developer pastes a production database password into a public GitHub issue. What do you do in the first hour?
p: Rotate the credential immediately, remove or redact the content (knowing it is already scraped), check database logs for use since exposure, invalidate sessions, and then fix the process with scanning and training.
cmds: psql -c "select usename, client_addr, backend_start from pg_stat_activity"
tip: Redaction does not help. Public content is scraped within minutes, so rotation is the only real remediation.
a: I treat the password as compromised from the moment it was posted. Step one is rotation: change the database credential and update the consumers, using the secret manager so the rollout is quick and safe. In parallel I ask the platform to delete or redact the comment and its edit history, and request cache purges, but I do not rely on that since automated scrapers collect public content within minutes. Then I investigate exposure: database logs and cloud audit logs for connections from unknown addresses since the time of posting, unusual queries or exports, and whether the account had network reachability from the internet at all. If misuse is found, it becomes a full incident with containment. I notify the data owner and, depending on data and regulations, privacy or legal teams. Afterwards I add secret scanning and push protection, correct the process, and coach the developer without blame.
f: Why doesn't deleting the comment fix it?

q: A scanner flags a critical CVE in a base image used by 80 services. How do you drive remediation at scale?
p: Confirm exploitability and exposure, rebuild the golden image with the patch, let a bot open PRs across services, prioritise internet-facing ones, track progress on a dashboard, and use admission policy to block old digests after the deadline.
cmds: gh search prs --owner acme 'bump base image' --state open
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{..image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | sort | uniq -c | grep old-digest
tip: Central base image plus automated update PRs turns an 80-repo problem into one patch and one rollout.
a: First I validate the finding: is the vulnerable component actually present and reachable in how our services use it, is there a known exploit, and which services are internet-facing. That sets urgency. Next I fix it once at the source: the platform team rebuilds the golden base image with the patched package, scans and signs it, and publishes a new digest. Then I use automation to propagate the change: a dependency bot opens pull requests in each repository bumping the base digest, and CI rebuilds, tests and deploys. I prioritise the exposed and most critical services, track progress on a dashboard listing which services still run the old digest, and chase owners of stragglers. To prevent indefinite lag, a policy blocks deployment of images built on bases older than a defined age after a deadline. If patching is delayed, I add compensating controls such as WAF rules or network restrictions.
f: How do you find all services using the old base?

q: Falco alerts that a shell was spawned in a production pod and an outbound connection to an unknown IP was made. Walk through your response.
p: Treat it as likely compromise. Preserve evidence, isolate the pod with network policy rather than deleting, capture logs and filesystem, identify the entry point, check lateral movement and credentials, then rebuild and rotate.
tip: Cordon the node and snapshot before deleting anything, so forensics remain possible.
a: A shell in a production container combined with an unexpected outbound connection is a strong indicator of compromise, so I act on it. First I contain without destroying evidence: apply a quarantine network policy that blocks the pod's ingress and egress, keep it running, and cordon the node if I suspect the host. I collect evidence: logs, the process list, network connections, the filesystem diff and, if possible, a memory image, and preserve the alert context. Then I scope the incident: what service account token and secrets the pod had, what cloud role it could assume, and whether those credentials were used elsewhere, using audit logs. I identify the entry point, such as a vulnerable endpoint or a leaked credential. Eradication means replacing the workload from a clean image, rotating all exposed secrets and tokens, and patching the weakness. Finally I tune detections and write a review.
f: Why not delete the pod immediately?
How do you scope lateral movement?

q: GuardDuty or a similar service reports crypto-mining on an EC2 instance. What is your process?
p: Verify the finding, isolate the instance, preserve snapshots, identify how it got in (exposed service, leaked key, vulnerable app), revoke credentials, hunt for other affected resources and persistence, then rebuild.
tip: Check for new IAM users, access keys, and additional instances in other regions. Attackers often persist and scale out.
a: I start by confirming the finding with network flow data, process information or CPU graphs, to avoid acting on a false alarm, but I do not delay containment for a likely true positive. I isolate the instance by switching to a quarantine security group, and revoke or rotate the credentials of its instance role, since a miner often arrives together with stolen credentials. I snapshot the volumes for forensics and keep the instance until evidence is captured. To find the root cause, I review how the host was reachable and what was running: an exposed management interface, a vulnerable web application, weak SSH credentials or leaked access keys. Then I hunt for scope using audit logs: new users, keys, roles, instances launched in unused regions, and changes to security settings. After cleanup I rebuild from a clean image, patch the entry point, enable guardrails like region restrictions, and set budget alerts.
f: How can billing alerts help detection?

q: You enforce a new admission policy and it blocks a critical production deployment during an incident. What do you do?
p: Restore service first using a documented, audited bypass or exception, then fix the root cause. Afterwards review why audit mode did not catch it and improve rollout, communication and escape hatches.
tip: Pre-agree the emergency path. During an incident, nobody should be inventing how to switch a policy to audit mode.
a: Service restoration comes first. A documented break-glass path should exist so that on-call engineers can switch the offending policy to audit mode, or add a narrowly scoped, time-limited exception, with approval recorded and an alert sent to the security team. I use it, get the deployment through, and confirm the incident is resolved. Then I analyse the cause: did the workload violate the rule legitimately, such as an old image running as root, or was the policy wrong or too broad? I fix whichever it is, either by remediating the manifest or by correcting the policy, and remove the temporary exception. In the retrospective I ask why my rollout missed it: audit mode should have surfaced this workload, perhaps the policy was enforced early or the reports were not reviewed. Improvements include better dry-run reports, staged rollout by namespace, clear communication, and drills of the emergency procedure.
f: What makes a safe break-glass path?

q: An auditor asks for evidence that all production changes were reviewed and approved in the last quarter. How do you produce it?
p: Query Git and the deployment system: list production deploys, map each to a merged PR with approvals and passing checks, flag exceptions such as emergency changes with retroactive review, and provide the protection settings as evidence.
cmds: gh pr list --state merged --base main --search 'merged:2026-07-01..2026-09-30' --json number,reviews,mergedBy --limit 500
tip: Automate the query so evidence takes minutes, and treat unreviewed changes as findings to explain, not hide.
a: I answer with data from systems of record, not screenshots. First I show the control design: the branch protection rules that require approval from someone other than the author, passing required checks, and no direct pushes, along with the audit log proving the settings were in place throughout the quarter. Then I demonstrate operation: from the deployment system, list every production deployment in the period, link each to the commit and merged pull request, and show approvals, reviewer identity and check results. A script flags anomalies such as merges without review, administrator bypasses and emergency changes. For those I present the emergency procedure and the retrospective approval record. An auditor will usually sample, so I can pull full evidence for any chosen change quickly. Transparency about exceptions builds credibility, and any gaps become tracked improvements, such as removing bypass rights.
f: How do you handle emergency changes?
Why prefer system records to screenshots?
